title: Evaluating New Information

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think about baking cookies. Gathering flour and sugar is collecting your stuff, choosing the recipe is deciding, and putting the tray in the oven is doing. Evaluation is when you open the oven and ask, "Did they turn out the way I expected?" You can only evaluate after you did something AND after you had an expectation to compare it to.

### Question 2

If you water a wilted plant, the point of checking it the next morning is not to prove you held the watering can. It is to see whether the leaves perked up. Re-assessing is that morning check: new information that tells you if what you did actually helped.

### Question 3

Imagine you packed a raincoat because the forecast said rain, then you step outside and it is sunny and 85 degrees. That sunshine is a new cue: a fresh fact that showed up after you made your plan and gives you a reason to change it.

### Question 4

Think of marking your height on a doorframe. The first pencil mark is the baseline; by itself it tells you nothing about growth. The second mark, months later, only means something because the first one is there. Evaluation is that second mark: it is a measurement whose meaning comes from what it is compared to.

### Question 5

Saying "I'll run better next week" is impossible to check. Saying "I'll run a mile in under ten minutes by next Friday" gives you a stopwatch number to look at. A measurable outcome hands you the stopwatch; a vague one leaves two people arguing about opinions with no way to settle it.

### Question 6

If you guess a friend is not answering because their phone is dead, and then you see them posting online, that post breaks your guess. Information that fits your explanation can never rule it out; only information that clashes with it can. That is why the clashing finding is the one worth chasing.

### Question 7

Imagine grading your own test but only checking the questions you already know you got right. Your score will look great and mean nothing. The fix is not working harder on the questions you like, it is deliberately going to the ones you might have missed.

### Question 8

If you promised to read 50 pages by Friday and you read 20, you did not read nothing and you did not finish. Calling it "done" hides the gap and calling it a failure throws away real progress. Naming it partway there is what points you toward the useful question: what slowed you down, and what should change?

### Question 9

Anyone can write down the score of a game. Integrating information is noticing your team has given up three goals in a row, deciding something about the defense is failing, and looking harder at that side of the field. The move is spotting a pattern and then going to collect more information about it.

### Question 10

A forecast that said "sunny" this morning was not wrong for saying it, but when clouds roll in you do not keep insisting it is sunny until the next scheduled forecast. You look again and update. A conclusion is tied to the moment it was drawn, so new conditions send you back through the reasoning, not around it.

### Question 11

Two judges watch the same dive and one calls it excellent while the other calls it mediocre. The dive did not change; the scoring rules in their heads did. Writing down in advance exactly what will count as success is how you get two people looking at the same thing to land on the same answer.

### Question 12

If your bread does not rise, the first question is not "is this recipe wrong?" It is "did I actually add the yeast?" You cannot judge whether something works until you know it was truly done. Checking that the plan was carried out as written protects you from throwing out a plan that was never really tried.
